title: The stone Buddhas
hook: at Gal Vihara in Polonnaruwa, great Buddhas carved from one rock, standing, seated, lying

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddhaghosa arrived and built a whole book on one verse. Your line was the commentator. Did you read one line slowly? Today, the teaching in stone instead of words. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

A long face of granite, in the old royal city of Polonnaruwa in Sri Lanka. Out of it, sculptors cut the Buddha: seated in meditation, standing with arms folded, and lying on his side. Nothing was carried in and set in place. The figures were uncovered, the stone around them cut away, so that each one is still part of the hill. The place is called Gal Vihara, the rock monastery.
screen: `ONE FACE OF GRANITE.` → `SEATED, STANDING, LYING.` → `GAL VIHARA.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The later chronicle credits King Parakramabahu with rebuilding Polonnaruwa as a royal city of parks, reservoirs and monasteries, and with the rock monastery itself. Second, the seated Buddha. He sits in meditation, hands resting in his lap, with a calm the stone holds without effort. Behind him the rock is carved with small details, as if he sits in a shrine of his own. Third, the standing figure, arms folded across his chest. Who is he? People disagree. Some say the Buddha himself, in the days after his awakening. Others say Ananda, his companion and attendant, standing in grief beside his dying teacher. The stone doesn't say, and the debate is still open. Fourth, the lying Buddha. In the account of the Buddha's last days, the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, he lies down on his right side, one foot resting on the other, mindful and clear, between two sal trees. The great reclining figure lies just that way, his head on a pillow. Some see a sleeping Buddha. Others see the final passing. The chronicle doesn't say why the sculptors chose to work in a single rock. What the stone itself shows is simple: nothing is stacked or joined. The figures share one body with the hill. And a stone Buddha does not fidget, does not check the time, does not shift its weight. Part of what people come for is to sit near that stillness for a while.
screen: `A KING'S ROCK MONASTERY.` · `SEATED, IN MEDITATION.` · `STANDING: THE BUDDHA, OR ANANDA?` · `LYING ON HIS RIGHT SIDE.` · then, large: `CARVED FROM ONE ROCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit like a stone Buddha. Find a steady seat, on a chair or on the floor. Let your hands rest in your lap. Let your back be upright without strain, the way stone is upright without trying. Now, for the length of the bell, try not to adjust. When an itch comes, or the urge to shift, notice it, and see whether it can pass the way weather passes over rock. If you need to move, move gently, and settle again. The bell holds the time.
The stone Buddhas. The figures of Gal Vihara in Polonnaruwa, seated, standing and lying, cut from a single face of rock. Today's word.
Your line: carved from one rock. Today, once, when you want to fidget or reach for your phone, stay still for a few breaths, like stone. Day eight hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Pilgrims at Gal Vihara remove their shoes, offer flowers and sit or stand quietly before the figures; in Buddhist temples, seated and reclining images serve as a focus for meditation and devotion.

fork.reveal: the Mahaparinibbana Sutta says he lay on his right side, one foot on the other, mindful and clear. the reclining figure at Gal Vihara lies the same way.

original.note: Pali: parinibbana, the Buddha's final passing, which the reclining figure is often read to show.

trapdoor: what you thought: separate statues set side by side.
what it means: figures cut from one face of granite: seated, standing and lying.
what a scholar hears: the later chronicle credits King Parakramabahu, and the standing figure is still debated: the Buddha, or Ananda in grief.
